title: Author a Subagent — and the Fork-Context Subtlety

questions.prompt: Your triage subagent declines most out-of-scope requests because its body says "you do one thing." Last week it still ran an unwanted shell command. What closes the gap?
options: Add an explicit refusal list to the body, covering each case you can think of
Narrow the description so out-of-scope work never routes here
Add Bash to disallowedTools, so the capability is gone rather than discouraged
Set maxTurns low, so the agent has less opportunity to wander
questions.explanation: A refusal list is still a request and you have to enumerate every case; the capability itself is what makes the request unnecessary. Option A lengthens a prompt that already failed. Option B is bypassed by any explicit @-mention, so it reduces wrong delegations but cannot prevent a wrong one. Option D limits how long it runs, not what it may do.

questions.prompt: You write max_turns: 10 in a subagent's frontmatter and the agent runs for thirty turns anyway. Why?
options: maxTurns only applies to subagents that set a model explicitly
maxTurns caps tool calls, not turns
The field is maxTurns; max_turns is unrecognized and silently ignored
maxTurns was capped at 5 in this version
questions.explanation: Unknown frontmatter keys are dropped with no warning, so the cap you thought you set was never applied — that's why nothing happened rather than something surprising. Option A and B invent rules that don't exist, and option D gives a cap that would have produced a partial return rather than unlimited running.

questions.prompt: A subagent you delegated to was supposed to be clean and focused on one narrow job. It came back quoting details from a decision you made twenty turns ago that it had no reason to see. What happened?
options: The subagent read your CLAUDE.md, which records recent decisions
Fork mode is on by default, so Claude spawned a fork that inherited your conversation
The delegation message quoted the conversation back to it
The subagent resumed a previous run with your history attached
questions.explanation: When Claude spawns a subagent without naming a type, it may spawn a fork — and a fork inherits the whole parent conversation plus system prompt, tools, and model, which is exactly the context you were trying to isolate it from. Option A is wrong because CLAUDE.md holds conventions, not conversation. Option C is Claude's summary of your *request*, not your history. Option D requires a resume you never performed.

questions.prompt: You wrote a reusable "run the release checklist" workflow. Running it dumped the whole checklist output into your conversation, which is fine — you want to act on each step as it comes. What should this have been?
options: A fork, so the checklist agent can see why each step exists
A skill, because the result belongs interleaved in your window
A subagent with maxTurns set high, so nothing gets truncated
A subagent with a skills field naming the checklist
questions.explanation: The deciding question is where the result should land: interleaved in your own conversation means a skill, and a skill runs in your window by design. A subagent exists to keep its mess out of yours — here you'd get a summary of steps you need to follow one at a time, which is the opposite of useful. Option A adds isolation cost for no benefit; options C and D are variations on a subagent, which is the wrong shape regardless of tuning.

questions.prompt: A subagent runs long searches across your whole repo and keeps running out of room on big ones. You never set a model. What's most likely?
options: It inherited your session's context window but lost track of the token count
Its context window comes from its own model's alias, which may be smaller than yours
Its window is fixed at 100k regardless of model, and you need autoCompactWindow
Subagents share one window pool across the session, so other agents ate its room
questions.explanation: A subagent's window is sized by the model named in its own `model` field, not the parent's — so delegating to a cheaper alias quietly gives it a smaller room, and a search that fits in yours may not fit in its. Option A describes the opposite relationship. Option C invents a fixed size. Option D is wrong because each non-fork subagent's context is isolated — that's the whole point of the phase.
